claim_checks.claim: Dartmouth BASIC prints a quoted message with <line number> PRINT "..."
claim_checks.evidence: BASIC manual 1 Oct 1964, p.28 §2.6.3 (form and examples); p.31 §3.1 rule 1 (a label in quotes is printed as it appears)

claim_checks.claim: A BASIC program needs END, and END has the highest line number
Every BASIC statement begins with a line number; numbering by tens matches the manual's own example
claim_checks.evidence: BASIC manual 1 Oct 1964, p.3 §2.1 (lines 10-90); p.56 Appendix C

claim_checks.claim: FORTRAN II PRINT takes a FORMAT statement number and prints on the on-line printer
PRINT 1 may omit the list when FORMAT 1 contains only alphameric (H) fields
claim_checks.evidence: C28-6054-5 p.22 excepts a FORMAT 'consists entirely of alphameric fields' from pairing with a list; the p.24 general form still shows a List and no list-free example was found. C28-6274-2 (7090 FORTRAN IV) p.21.1 says PRINT requires an output list, so the sample is not labelled FORTRAN IV.

claim_checks.claim: 6H HELLO is six characters: a leading blank plus HELLO; blanks count in w
claim_checks.evidence: C28-6054-5 p.21 (wH, blanks included in the count)

claim_checks.claim: The first character of a printed record is carriage control, not printed; blank means single space; one H field may hold the control character and the text
claim_checks.evidence: C28-6054-5 p.22 (Carriage Control, required for PRINT); p.5 Figure 1-1 uses 22H1THE LARGEST OF THESE and 12H NUMBERS IS

claim_checks.claim: Under the FORTRAN II Monitor a program ends with CALL EXIT, not STOP, and END is still required as the physically last card
claim_checks.evidence: C28-6054-5 p.34 item 4b-c; p.16 (STOP not for Monitor/IBSYS; END last); p.40 (plain END allowed); p.5 Figure 1-1 ends CALL EXIT / END

claim_checks.claim: Statement numbers in card columns 1-5, statements from column 7
Every character in the FORTRAN listing is in the FORTRAN II source character set
claim_checks.evidence: C28-6054-5 p.46 Appendix B (letters, digits, blank, parentheses)

claim_checks.claim: Script SCRIPT.md:69: the BASIC version is visibly shorter
claim_checks.evidence: Same task, no padding: FORTRAN II needs 4 statements, BASIC 2, at identical 48 px code size. Every FORTRAN line is required (F1-F5). The gap is two lines for a minimal program; this asset does not show that it holds for larger programs.

claim_checks.claim: Script SCRIPT.md:69: the BASIC version is more readable
claim_checks.evidence: Judgement. Checkable differences are shown instead: FORTRAN needs a separate FORMAT statement, counted Hollerith text, a carriage-control character and card columns; BASIC puts the message in quotes on one numbered line.

claim_checks.claim: Script SCRIPT.md:71 narration: 1964 languages, punched cards, Kemeny and Kurtz's aims
claim_checks.evidence: Nothing in these exports states these points. Incidentally confirmed: the BASIC manual is dated 1 October 1964 by the Dartmouth College Computation Center, and C28-6054-5 p.5 describes punching each FORTRAN statement on a card. Kemeny and Kurtz are not named on the pages read.

claim_checks.claim: Either sample ran on period hardware or produced output
claim_checks.evidence: No execution environment was used; the exports show source text only and no output or compile result.

review_questions.question: The FORTRAN II sample uses PRINT 1 with no output list. IBM's 7090/7094 FORTRAN II manual allows an all-alphameric FORMAT without a list but shows no list-free PRINT example, and nothing was executed. Accept it as an illustrative listing, or should an emulator run be commissioned before release? Adding a dummy variable to the list would pad FORTRAN and is not recommended.

resolution.decision: 'More readable' stays in narration as the narrator's judgement; the frame itself makes no readability claim.
